articles.title: How to Calculate How Much Drywall You Need (And the Mud to Go With It)
articles.excerpt: Buying drywall is a guessing game. You buy too few sheets and the store is out of stock. You forget to factor in the ceiling. You never know exactly how much joint compound or screws to buy. Let's loo…
articles.body: Buying drywall is a guessing game. You buy too few sheets and the store is out of stock. You forget to factor in the ceiling. You never know exactly how much joint compound or screws to buy. Let's look at how to automate the calculation using JavaScript. The Math (Step-by-Step) Calculate Total Area: (Wall Height × Total Wall Length) + (Ceiling Length × Ceiling Width) = Total Square Feet Divide by Sheet Size: Total Area ÷ 32 = Number of 4x8 Sheets (or divide by 48 for 4x12 sheets). Add Waste Factor: Multiply by 1.10 (10% waste) for standard rooms, or 1.15 (15%) for rooms with lots of corners. Estimate Materials: Screws: 1 lb per 300 sq ft. Joint Compound: 1 gallon per 100 sq ft. Tape: 1 roll (500 ft) per 1,000 sq ft.

articles.title: Modern JavaScript: Variables, Functions and Objects
articles.excerpt: All JavaScript looks the same, and a good chunk of it is wrong. Not broken — dated. Code written in 2012 and pasted into 2026, full of underscores, callbacks and var everywhere, like a family recipe n…
articles.body: All JavaScript looks the same, and a good chunk of it is wrong. Not broken — dated. Code written in 2012 and pasted into 2026, full of underscores, callbacks and var everywhere, like a family recipe nobody has updated and everybody keeps cooking. You're going to read a lot of it, so it pays to know what's dated and what isn't. There's a better reason too: almost everything in JavaScript that looks arbitrary has a specific explanation behind it. const that isn't constant. this that changes with the way you call. class that isn't a class. Every one of those oddities is a design decision, and until you see it, the language looks like it was written by someone in a hurry. It was. But it's consistent.

articles.title: How to Calculate Real Throughput in an Automated Filling Line

articles.body: A filling machine rated at 100 bottles per minute does not necessarily mean a production line can deliver 6,000 finished bottles every hour. In an automated packaging system, actual throughput depends on more than the filling unit. Bottle handling, capping, labeling, inspection, product characteristics, changeovers, and unplanned downtime all influence the number of acceptable products leaving the line. For manufacturing engineers and production managers, understanding this difference is essential when evaluating equipment investments. This article explains a practical method for estimating real production throughput using line balancing, bottleneck analysis, and Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE). 1.

articles.title: Your RAG Agent Cites Sources. Check That the Quotes Are Real.
articles.excerpt: A small Python quote check that catches made-up citations before a user sees them, and the one trap I hit while building it. A citation makes an answer look trustworthy. But a model can attach a real…
articles.body: A small Python quote check that catches made-up citations before a user sees them, and the one trap I hit while building it. A citation makes an answer look trustworthy. But a model can attach a real document ID to a sentence that is not in that document. Or it can quote the document almost perfectly, with one number changed. Both look fine in the UI. When I build agents that answer from documents, I don't trust a citation until code has checked it. Here is the small check I use, and a bug I found in my own first version while writing this post. Ask for quotes, not just document IDs A citation that only says "source: policy-7" cannot be checked. You would need another model call to decide whether the claim is supported.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 15, 1988: The 300-foot Green Bank Telescope collapses suddenly, leaving a huge pile of wreckage in West Virginia
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. It happened at 9:46 p.m. on a clear night with no strong winds. When the observatory staff showed up to work the next morning, they were greeted by a huge pile of wreckage. The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed. This was one of four connecting plates that held the telescope's large, metal beams together. Investigators found that these gusset plates were not built to last the 26 years that this telescope had been in use. Three years later, construction began on a new telescope. The Green Bank Telescope was even bigger and more sensitive, and it began science operations in 2001.

articles.excerpt: "T CrB *will* erupt sometime soon. Everyone is very confident on this."
articles.body: For the past two years, stargazers have waited with bated breath for a "new" light to appear in the night sky, born of one of the most cataclysmic events known to occur in the cosmos — a nova explosion. But what is the "Blaze Star" T. Coronae Borealis, and why is it so difficult to predict when its overdue brightening will occur? We turned to the experts to find out. What is T. Coronae Borealis? T. Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant. Over a period of around 80 years, the white dwarf's gravity strips material from the red giant until it hits a critical threshold.

articles.title: How escaping gases ripped apart a comet and caused it to become thousands of times brighter
articles.excerpt: This summer, comet 220P/McNaught burst into life out of nowhere to become one of the year’s highlights for amateur astronomers.
articles.body: A comet dazzled this summer as the sun’s heat caused ice beneath its surface to turn to gas and rip out through its surface, spewing hundreds of billions of pounds' worth of dust into space and causing the comet to brighten by thousands of times. Comet 220P/McNaught was discovered by the prolific Australian comet discoverer Robert McNaught in 2004. It is a periodic comet, the 220th discovered, meaning that it comes back again and again on a regular basis – in 220P’s case, once every five-and-a-half years when it gets about as close to the sun as Mars . Other than that, 220P is fairly nondescript, usually languishing at a feeble brightness fainter than magnitude +15, out of reach of most amateur telescopes. There has been little else to say about the comet, until this year.
